Tadao Ando

Church of the Light (1989) Main Objective * Explore how natural light can create a spiritual atmosphere in architecture. * Demonstrate how simple geometry and minimal materials can produce powerful spatial experiences. Key Facts * Located in Ibaraki, Osaka, Japan. * Designed by Tadao Ando and completed in 1989. * Simple rectangular concrete volume * Famous cross-shaped opening in the wall behind the altar. * Natural light enters through the cross, creating a strong symbolic and spiritual effect.

Rokko Housing (1983) Main Objective • Integrate housing into a steep natural landscape while preserving views and minimizing disruption to nature. Key Facts * Located in Kobe, Japan, on the slopes of the Rokko Mountains. * Designed by Tadao Ando. * Built on a 60-degree hillside slope. * Apartments arranged in stepped concrete terraces following the slope. * Each unit has views toward Osaka Bay. * Emphasizes geometry, landscape integration, and outdoor terraces.

Chichu Art Museum (2004) Main Objective • Create a museum where architecture, light, and art work together to shape the visitor's experience. Key Facts * Located on Naoshima Island, Japan. * Designed by Tadao Ando and completed in 2004. * Built mostly underground to preserve the natural landscape. * Uses geometric forms (squares, triangles, circles). * Galleries illuminated only by natural light. * Features artworks by Claude Monet, Walter De Maria, and James Turrell.

Barcelona Pavilion ● Space is broken down through arrangement of large floor to ceiling glass panes, metal columns, and travertine walls (becoming the new material and formal palette of modern design). ● Integration of screens help guide circulation and create new. semi-transparent view points ● Composition of surfaces and materials sets precedent for a blurred relationship between indoor and outdoor space. The Barcelona Pavilion Barcelona, Spain Originally constructed in 1928, later reconstructed in 1986

Barcelona Chair ● Chrome-plated steel frame defines new modern material palette of reimagined industrial materials. ● Contextualization in minimalist interior draws emphasis to the chair and defines furniture as integral elements to architectural interiors. ● Integration of furniture with the pavilion’s spatial condition sets precedent for spatial hierarchy in modern interior architecture. The Barcelona Chair First manufactured in Berlin Germany, showcased in Barcelona, Spain Created in 1929

Muzharul Islam 1

Faculty of Fine Arts (Institute of Fine Arts), Dhaka,1953-1956 Muzharul Islam, Faculty of Fine Arts, Shahbagh, Dhaka, 1953–56, site plan (Muzharul Islam archive, University of Asia Pacific, Dhaka, http://www.muzharulislam.com). Muzharul Islam, Faculty of Fine Arts, Shahbagh, Dhaka, 1953-56 (photo by A. Q. M. Abdullah, 2004; Zainab F. Ali and Fuad H. Mallick, eds., Muzharul Islam, [Dhaka: BRAC University Press, 2011]). One of the first modernist buildings in Bangladesh and Islam’s first major project. Rejects colonial architectural styles and religious symbolism. Uses locally sourced brick, reducing maintenance and reflecting local construction traditions. Building layout preserves existing trees and landscape in Shahbag. Circulation spaces and courtyards connect indoor learning with outdoor nature. Adapts international modernism to the environmental and cultural context of Bangladesh.

3 Jahangirnagar University,Dhaka,1967–1970 Muzharul Islam, Jahangirnagar University, Dhaka, Bangladesh,plan, 1967-1970 Campus master plan designed to minimize environmental disruption. Buildings carefully oriented for natural ventilation and balanced sun exposure in Bangladesh’s hot climate. Triangular and faceted building forms respond to climate and spatial logic. Courtyards and open spaces encourage social interaction and community life. Continues Islam’s use of brick construction with traditional patterns. Demonstrates how modernist design can be adapted to local climate and culture. Muzharul Islam, Jahangirnagar University, Dhaka, Bangladesh,close up, 1967-1970

4 Chittagong University,Chittagong,1965-1975 Designed for hilly and mountainous terrain of the Chittagong region. Islam studied monsoon patterns and drainage systems before planning the campus. Buildings placed in valleys to preserve natural water flow and prevent landslides. Site planning protects the ecological system and landscape. Rectangular building forms provide efficient classroom and learning spaces. Demonstrates Islam’s principle of working with the environment rather than against it. Muzharul Islam.
